examples: The museum's exposition of modern art attracted thousands of visitors.
The book opens with a clear exposition of its central theory.
etymology: from Latin expositio, from ex- (out) + ponere/posit- (place) + -ion; literally 'a placing out'.

similar.description: both begin with ex- but 'exposition' is explanation, 'exposure' is uncovering/display.

memory_tip: ex(出)+posit(放)+ion → 把内容“摆放出来”即阐述、展览。

examples: His expulsion from the school followed repeated rule-breaking.
The expulsion of the intruder restored order.
etymology: from Latin expulsio, from ex- (out) + pellere/puls- (drive) + -ion; 'a driving out'.

similar.description: both involve pushing away; expulsion is forced removal, repulsion is disgust or physical pushback.

memory_tip: ex(出)+pel(推) → 推出去即驱逐、开除。

examples: The campaign aimed to exterminate the invasive rodent population.
We must exterminate the termites before they ruin the wood.
etymology: from Latin exterminare, from ex- (out) + terminus (boundary) + -are; originally 'drive beyond the boundary'.

similar.description: share root termin- (end); exterminate means destroy utterly, terminate means end.

memory_tip: ex+termin(边界) → 赶到边界之外彻底消灭。

examples: Grab the fire extinguisher in case the pan catches flame.
Each floor is equipped with a foam extinguisher.
etymology: from Latin exstinguere, from ex- (out) + stinguere (quench) + -er (agent noun).

similar.description: both contain -sting-; distinguish means tell apart, extinguisher puts out fire.

memory_tip: ex+sting(熄) → 把火“刺熄”的工具即灭火器。

examples: Critics extol the novel as a masterpiece of the decade.
She never tired of extolling her teacher's virtues.
etymology: from Latin extollere, from ex- (out) + tollere (raise/lift); 'lift up' in praise.

similar.description: similar opening; extol praises, extort coerces unlawfully.

memory_tip: 把人“举起来”(extol)夸赞，记住是褒义。

examples: The gang tried to extort money from local shopkeepers.
He was jailed for attempting to extort a confession.
etymology: from Latin extorquere, from ex- (out) + torquere (twist); 'wring out' by force.

similar.description: both use root tort/torqu (twist); distort means deform, extort means coerce.

memory_tip: twist out money → 敲诈、勒索。

examples: The children were exuberant at the news of the trip.
Her exuberant energy lit up the room.
etymology: from Latin exuberare, from ex- (out) + uber (fruitful/abundant); 'overflowing with abundance'.

similar.description: both start ex-; exuberant is lively/abundant, exotic is foreign.

memory_tip: ex+uber(丰盛) → 洋溢出来的丰盛 → 精力充沛的。

examples: She kept a careful eye on the simmering pot.
The storm's eye passed directly over the island.
etymology: from Old English eage, from Proto-Germanic *augon; akin to Latin oculus.
memory_tip: 古英语eage，联想“eye”像眼睛形状。

examples: He tried to save face after the embarrassing mistake.
The north face of the mountain is the hardest to climb.
etymology: from Latin facies (form, appearance, face), from facere (make/do).

similar.description: facet is a small face/side of a gem, derived from face.

memory_tip: 来自拉丁facere(做)→表面、脸面。

examples: Each facet of the diamond caught the light differently.
We examined every facet of the problem.
etymology: from French facette, diminutive of face (face); literally 'little face/side'.

similar.description: facet is a small face/side, from French facette.

memory_tip: face的小面 → 宝石的刻面、问题的方面。

examples: The archive sent a facsimile of the original letter.
A facsimile edition reproduces the book page for page.
etymology: from Latin fac simile 'make similar', from facere (make) + similis (like).

similar.description: contains simile/simil (like); facsimile is an exact copy.

memory_tip: fac(做)+simile(相似) → 做成相似的 → 复制品。

examples: Please give me the factual details, not opinions.
The report is factual and well documented.
etymology: from Latin factum (thing done/deed) + -ual; 'of facts'.

similar.description: factual is real/true, fictional is invented.

memory_tip: fact(事实)+ual → 基于事实的。

examples: Water boils at 212 degrees Fahrenheit.
The Fahrenheit scale is still used in the US.
etymology: named after German physicist Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit (1686–1736), who devised the temperature scale.

similar.description: both are temperature scales; Fahrenheit is the older non-metric one.

memory_tip: 华伦海特(Fahrenheit)命名的温标，记住大写F。

examples: Leaves fall from the trees in autumn.
The fall of the empire took centuries.
etymology: from Old English feallan, from Proto-Germanic *fallan; akin to Latin fallere.

similar.description: fell can be past of fall or mean cut down; watch tense.

memory_tip: 古英语feallan，落下、跌倒、秋天（美式）。

examples: The argument rests on a logical fallacy.
It is a fallacy that eating fat makes you fat.
etymology: from Latin fallacia, from fallere (deceive/be mistaken); 'deception'.

similar.description: both from fall- (err/deceive); fallacy is a false belief, fallible means can err.

memory_tip: fall(欺骗/错) → 谬误、错误推理。

examples: Even experts are fallible and make mistakes.
The system is fallible despite its safeguards.
etymology: from Medieval Latin fallibilis, from fallere (deceive/err) + -ibilis (able); 'able to err'.

similar.description: share fall- root; fallible means capable of error, fallacy is an error itself.

memory_tip: fall(犯错)+ible(能) → 会犯错的、易错的。

examples: He was fired for trying to falsify the records.
Witnesses alleged the document had been falsified.
etymology: from Latin falsificare, from falsus (false) + facere (make); 'make false'.

similar.description: antonyms: falsify makes false, verify confirms truth.

memory_tip: false+ify → 弄假、篡改。

examples: His familiarity with the software impressed the interviewer.
Familiarity bred contempt between the rivals.
etymology: from Latin familiaris (of a household/family) + -ity; 'state of being well known'.

similar.description: both from Latin familia (household); familiarity is closeness of knowledge.

memory_tip: familiar(熟悉)+ity → 熟悉程度。

examples: A fanatic of the band queued for days.
His fanatic devotion alarmed his friends.
etymology: from Latin fanaticus 'of a temple, inspired by deity', from fanum (temple); later 'frantic, zealous'.

similar.description: both from temple-ecstasy roots; fanatic is zealot, frantic is panicked.

memory_tip: 神庙狂热者 → 狂热分子、极端分子。

examples: The documentary offered a fascinating look at deep-sea life.
Her story was absolutely fascinating.
etymology: from Latin fascinare (bewitch/charm) + -ing; 'casting a spell'.

similar.description: different roots; fascinating charms, fashion is style.

memory_tip: fascin(迷住)+ing → 迷人的、极有趣的。

examples: She is fastidious about cleanliness.
A fastidious editor caught every typo.
etymology: from Latin fastidiosus, from fastidium (loathing/disgust), from fastus (disdain) + taedium.

similar.description: both end -ious; fastidious is picky, tedious is boring.

memory_tip: 过分挑剔到令人生厌 → 吹毛求疵的。

examples: I cannot fathom why he would lie.
The lake is six fathoms deep.
etymology: from Old English fæthm 'armspan (length of two arms)', used as a measure of depth.

similar.description: unrelated; fathom is depth/comprehend, faith is belief.

memory_tip: 原指“伸开双臂”的长度 → 测量深度，引申为理解。

examples: Cut back on fatty foods to protect your heart.
The tissue was diagnosed as a fatty deposit.
etymology: from Middle English fat + -y; 'of or like fat'.

similar.description: unrelated; fatty concerns fat, fate is destiny.

memory_tip: fat(脂肪)+y → 含脂肪的、油腻的。

examples: His fatuous grin suggested he understood nothing.
She made a fatuous comment about the crisis.
etymology: from Latin fatuus 'foolish, silly'; akin to fari (speak).

similar.description: similar look; fatuous is silly, factual is true.

memory_tip: 来自拉丁fat(傻) → 愚昧的、傻的。

examples: The island's fauna includes rare reptiles.
Desert fauna have adapted to scarce water.
etymology: from Latin Fauna, sister of Faunus (rural deity), used for animal life of a region.

similar.description: flora is plant life, fauna is animal life of a region.

memory_tip: 动物群(fauna)对应植物群(flora)，f开头一对。

examples: Could you do me a small favour?
The weather favoured our picnic plans.
etymology: from Latin favor 'goodwill, support', from favere (favor/be kind).

similar.description: different words; favour is kindness, flavor is taste.

memory_tip: favere(喜爱) → 好感、帮忙、偏爱。

examples: I feel a draught near the window.
She felt proud of her son.
etymology: from Old English felan, from Proto-Germanic *fōlijan; akin to Latin palpare (touch).
memory_tip: 古英语felan，触摸、感觉。

examples: The femur is the longest bone in the body.
He fractured his femur in the fall.
etymology: from Latin femur (thigh); from Proto-Indo-European *fem- (to swell).

similar.description: both leg bones; femur is thigh bone, fibula is the smaller lower-leg bone.

memory_tip: 拉丁“大腿” → 股骨。

examples: He fended off the attacker with an umbrella.
Children must learn to fend for themselves.
etymology: from Old English fendan 'defend', shortened from defendan (defend).

similar.description: fend is a clipped form of defend; both mean protect/ward off.

memory_tip: defend的缩略 → 抵挡、照料自己。

examples: Fermentation turns grape juice into wine.
The dough rose through natural fermentation.
etymology: from Latin fermentum (leaven/yeast) + -ation; from fervere (boil).

similar.description: similar; fermentation is biochemical, fomentation is stirring up trouble.

memory_tip: ferve(沸腾)+ment → 发酵（像在冒泡）。

examples: A ferocious storm battered the coast.
The ferocious dog guarded the yard.
etymology: from Latin ferox 'wild, fierce' + -ous; from ferus (wild).

similar.description: both mean intense violence; ferocious is savagely wild, furious is angrily violent.

memory_tip: fer(野)+ocious → 凶猛的、残忍的。

examples: She made a fervent plea for peace.
His fervent support never wavered.
etymology: from Latin fervens, from ferveve (boil, glow); 'hot, burning'.

similar.description: same root; fervent is adjective (ardent), fervor is the noun (passion).

memory_tip: 内心像沸腾(ferve) → 热烈的、炽热的。

examples: The wound began to fester in the heat.
Resentment festered for years.
etymology: from Old English fysten 'to rot, suppurate'; akin to fūl (foul).

similar.description: unrelated; fester rots, faster is comparative of fast.

memory_tip: 伤口“腐烂化脓” → 恶化、积怨。

examples: The festivity continued late into the night.
We joined the festivities in the town square.
etymology: from Latin festivitas, from festus (festive/holiday) + -ity; from festum (feast).

similar.description: both from feast; festivity is celebration, festival is the event.

memory_tip: feast(宴)+ivity → 喜庆、欢庆。

examples: The prisoner's fetters clanked as he walked.
Bad habits can fetter the mind.
etymology: from Old English fetor 'chain for the feet'; from Proto-Germanic *fetero.

similar.description: unrelated; fetter is a shackle, better is comparative.

memory_tip: 脚镣 → 束缚、羁绊。

examples: The fetus develops rapidly in the third month.
Ultrasound showed a healthy fetus.
etymology: from Latin fetus 'offspring, bringing forth'; from Proto-Indo-European *dhe(i)- (to suck).

similar.description: foetus is a British spelling variant of fetus.

memory_tip: 拉丁“后代、胎儿” → 胎儿。

examples: A bitter feud divided the two families.
The feud over the land lasted decades.
etymology: from Middle English fede, from Old French feide, from Frankish *fēhida; akin to Old English fāh (hostile).

similar.description: unrelated; feud is a vendetta, fuel is combustible material.

memory_tip: 世仇、长期争斗，联想feudal(封建)时代的家族仇杀。

examples: Her fiance proposed on the beach.
He introduced his fiance to the family.
etymology: from French fiancé, past participle of fiancer 'to betroth', from fiance 'a promise'.

similar.description: similar start; fiance is a betrothed man, finance is money management.

memory_tip: 法语“已订婚的男子” → 未婚夫（女为fiancee）。

examples: Dietary fibre aids digestion.
The rope is made of strong natural fibre.
etymology: from Latin fibra 'thread, fibre'; of unknown earlier origin.

similar.description: fiber is the US spelling of fibre.

memory_tip: 拉丁“纤维、细丝” → 纤维。

examples: The fickle wind kept changing direction.
Voters can be fickle and unpredictable.
etymology: from Old English ficel 'deceitful, treacherous'; from fāc (deceit).

similar.description: similar ending; fickle is changeable, tickle is to lightly touch.

memory_tip: 易变而“狡诈” → 反复无常的。

examples: The recording lacks fidelity to the original.
He valued fidelity in a friend.
etymology: from Latin fidelitas, from fidelis (faithful), from fides (faith/trust).

similar.description: both from fides (faith); fidelity is loyalty, federal is alliance-based government.

memory_tip: fides(信任) → 忠实、保真度。

examples: Stop fidgeting during the meeting.
The child was a bundle of fidgets.
etymology: from frequentative of Old English *fīcian 'to move restlessly'; imitative of restless motion.

similar.description: unrelated; fidget is restlessness, widget is a gadget.

memory_tip: 坐立不安、小动作多，拟声感。

examples: A filament glows inside the light bulb.
The spider spun a fine filament of silk.
etymology: from Latin filum (thread) + -ment (noun suffix); 'a little thread'.

similar.description: share fil- (thread) root; filament is a thread, file is a tool or record.

memory_tip: fil(线)+ament → 细丝、灯丝。

examples: The alley was covered in filth.
He wiped the filth from his boots.
etymology: from Old English fylth, from fūl (foul); 'foulness'.

similar.description: unrelated; filth is dirt, faith is belief.

memory_tip: foul(脏) → 污秽、肮脏。

examples: He is finicky about the temperature of his coffee.
A finicky eater rejects many foods.
etymology: from fine + -icky (diminutive/pejorative suffix); 'overly concerned with fine points'.

similar.description: near synonyms; finicky is fussy, especially over detail.

memory_tip: fine(细)+icky → 过分讲究细节的、挑剔的。

examples: The suspect was found with a concealed firearm.
Gun control restricts the sale of firearms.
etymology: compound of fire + arm (weapon); a weapon that fires projectiles by gunpowder.

similar.description: distinguish from 'fire arm' (arm on fire); it is a gun.

memory_tip: fire(火)+arm(武器) → 火器、枪械。

examples: The jacket is a perfect fit.
He is fit for the demanding role.
etymology: from Old English fitt 'conflict, song'; modern senses from Middle English 'suitable'.

similar.description: fit is adjective/noun, fitness is the state of being fit.

memory_tip: 合适、健康、适合，多义核心“契合”。

examples: His arms grew flabby after months without exercise.
Avoid flabby arguments in your essay.
etymology: from flab (loose flesh, imitative) + -by; 'soft, limp'.

similar.description: both begin flab-; flabby is soft, flabbergasted is astonished.

memory_tip: 松软的肉 → 松弛的、不结实的。

examples: The path was paved with flat flagstones.
They sat on a cool flagstone in the garden.
etymology: from flag (a flat stone, of obscure origin) + stone; a flat paving slab.

similar.description: shares flag- (flat slab); flagstone is a paving stone.

memory_tip: flag(扁平石板)+stone → 铺路石板。

examples: Snow began to flake down at dusk.
He brushed a flake of paint from his sleeve.
etymology: from Old English flac 'flat stone/flake'; of Germanic origin, 'a flat thin piece'.

similar.description: unrelated; flake is a thin piece, slack is loose.

memory_tip: 扁平薄片 → 薄片、雪片。

examples: The hill guarded the army's left flank.
She flanked the table with two chairs.
etymology: from Old French flanc 'side of body', from Frankish *hlanka; akin to link.

similar.description: unrelated; flank is side, blank is empty.

memory_tip: 身体的侧边 → 侧翼、侧面。

examples: He carried water in a metal flask.
The chemist poured the acid into a flask.
etymology: from Old French flasque, from Medieval Latin flasca; of Germanic origin.

similar.description: similar start; flask is a bottle, flash is sudden light.

memory_tip: 细颈瓶、水壶，联想实验室烧瓶。

examples: She flaunted her new ring to everyone.
Don't flaunt your wealth so openly.
etymology: 16th century, of uncertain origin; perhaps from Scandinavian; 'display ostentatiously'.

similar.description: often confused; flaunt means show off, flout means defy/scorn rules.

memory_tip: 炫耀(flaunt)≠蔑视(flout)，记flaunt带a像“亮出来”。

examples: The soup has a rich garlic flavour.
Local dishes have a distinctive flavour.
etymology: from Old French flavor 'smell, taste', from Latin flatus (a blowing); 'aroma'.

similar.description: similar; flavour is taste, favour is kindness.

memory_tip: 气味、滋味 → 风味、口味。

examples: We caught a fleeting glimpse of the deer.
Fame can be fleeting.
etymology: from Old English fleotan 'float, flow' + -ing; 'passing like a flowing thing'.

similar.description: similar; fleeting is brief, fleeing is running away.

memory_tip: 像流水般掠过 → 短暂的、转瞬即逝的。

examples: He flicked the switch with his thumb.
She flicked the dust off the book.
etymology: late 16th century, imitative of a light, quick movement.

similar.description: both short sharp sounds; flick is a flip, click is a press/sound.

memory_tip: 轻弹、快速一甩，拟声动作。

examples: Candlelight flickered in the draught.
A faint hope flickered in her mind.
etymology: from Old English flicorian 'to flutter'; imitative of wavering light/motion.

similar.description: flicker is a repeated wavering flick; flick is one quick motion.

memory_tip: flick的反复 → 闪烁、摇曳。

examples: The flimsy tent collapsed in the wind.
He offered a flimsy excuse for being late.
etymology: 18th century, origin uncertain; perhaps from flim (thin sheet) + -sy; 'weak, frail'.

similar.description: distinguish from 'filmy' (thin film); flimsy is weak/frail.

memory_tip: 薄弱的、易坏的，联想薄纸。

examples: He flipped the pancake with a spatula.
She flipped the page impatiently.
etymology: 17th century, imitative of a light, sudden turn; 'toss or turn over'.

similar.description: related motion words; flip is turn over, flop is fall heavily.

memory_tip: 轻快翻转 → 抛、翻转。

examples: He flirted with the idea of quitting.
She flirted with him at the party.
etymology: 16th century, perhaps imitative of a brisk movement; originally 'to move jerkily'.

similar.description: similar; flirt is playful romance, flit is dart about.

memory_tip: 调情、轻率对待（想法），记轻佻动作。

examples: The region's flora includes alpine wildflowers.
Tropical flora thrives in the rainforest.
etymology: from Latin Flora, goddess of flowers; used for plant life of a region.

similar.description: flora is plant life, fauna is animal life.

memory_tip: 植物群(flora)对应动物群(fauna)，花神Flora。

examples: She brushed the fluff off her sweater.
The speech was full of fluff and little substance.
etymology: 18th century, perhaps imitative; 'soft, light particles'.

similar.description: fluff is the noun, fluffy is the adjective (soft).

memory_tip: 绒毛、蓬松物，拟声轻柔。

examples: The room was lit by fluorescent tubes.
A fluorescent vest glows under headlights.
etymology: from Latin fluo (flow) + -escent (becoming); named for glow that appears to 'flow'.

similar.description: share -escent; fluorescent glows, efflorescent blooms/flowers out.

memory_tip: flu(流)+escent → 发光的、荧光的。

examples: A butterfly fluttered past the window.
Her heart fluttered with nerves.
etymology: from Old English floterian, frequentative of fleotan (float); imitative of flapping.

similar.description: unrelated; flutter is flapping, flatter is praising insincerely.

memory_tip: 拍翅、飘动，拟声flap。

examples: The patient's condition is in a state of flux.
Magnetic flux was measured by the sensor.
etymology: from Latin fluxus 'flowing', from fluere (to flow); 'a flowing, continuous change'.

similar.description: both from fluere (flow); flu is illness, flux is flow/change.

memory_tip: flow(流) → 流动、不断变化的状况。

examples: The new flyover eased the morning traffic.
We drove beneath the flyover at dawn.
etymology: compound of fly + over; a bridge carrying one road over another.

similar.description: near synonym; flyover/overpass is an elevated road crossing.

memory_tip: fly(飞)+over → 立交桥、高架（车“飞过”）。

examples: Forgetting names is his only foible.
We tolerated each other's foibles.
etymology: from French faible 'weak', from Latin flebilis (lamentable); 'a minor weakness'.

similar.description: both from weak-root; foible is a small fault, feeble is weak.

memory_tip: 小弱点 → 小缺点、怪癖。

examples: The hero's courage was a foil to the villain's cruelty.
Wrap the cheese in aluminium foil.
etymology: verb 'to thwart' from Old French fouler 'to trample'; noun 'metal sheet' from Latin folium (leaf).

similar.description: unrelated; foil is thwart/metal leaf, forest is woods.

memory_tip: foil作“箔/衬托”或“挫败”，联想foil纸反光。

examples: The lab is at the forefront of cancer research.
She stayed in the forefront of public attention.
etymology: from fore- (before) + front; 'the very front, leading position'.

similar.description: forefront is the foremost front; front is the general front.

memory_tip: fore(前)+front → 最前沿、领先地位。

examples: Forensic evidence convicted the suspect.
She studied forensic science at university.
etymology: from Latin forensis 'of the forum', from forum (public place/court); 'pertaining to courts'.

similar.description: both from forum; forensic relates to legal/court inquiry.

memory_tip: forum(论坛/法庭) → 法医的、法庭的。

examples: The telegraph was a forerunner of the internet.
He is seen as a forerunner of modern art.
etymology: from fore- (before) + runner; 'one who runs ahead, a predecessor'.

similar.description: similar; forerunner precedes, predecessor held the role before.

memory_tip: fore(前)+runner → 先驱、前兆。

examples: The signing was a mere formality.
We observed the formalities of the ceremony.
etymology: from Latin formalis (of form) + -ity; 'adherence to form/ritual'.

similar.description: formality is the noun of formal observance, from form.

memory_tip: formal(正式的)+ity → 礼节、形式。

examples: The old fort guarded the harbour.
They retreated to the safety of the fort.
etymology: from Old French fort 'strong place', from Latin fortis (strong).

similar.description: fort is a stronghold, forte is one's strength; often confused.

memory_tip: fortis(强) → 堡垒、要塞。

examples: Cooking is her forte.
Debate is not my forte.
etymology: from French fort 'strong' (masculine); 'one's strong point'.

similar.description: often confused; forte is a strength, fort is a fortress.

memory_tip: 强项、特长，注意与fort(堡垒)区分。

examples: They fortified the wall with stone.
A hot meal fortified the travellers.
etymology: from Latin fortificare, from fortis (strong) + facere (make); 'make strong'.

similar.description: share fort- (strong); fortify is to strengthen, fort is the stronghold.

memory_tip: fort(强)+ify(使) → 加固、强化。

examples: Prices rose only fractionally this year.
The dial moved fractionally to the left.
etymology: from Latin fractio (breaking) + -al + -ly; 'by a small part/fraction'.

similar.description: fractionally is the adverb form of fraction.

memory_tip: fraction(一小部分)+ally → 略微、极小地。

examples: The fragrance of roses filled the garden.
She wore a light floral fragrance.
etymology: from Latin fragrantia, from fragrare (to smell sweet); 'sweet smell'.

similar.description: unrelated; fragrance is scent, flagrance is not a standard word (flagrant is shocking).

memory_tip: fragr(散发香味) → 芳香、香气。

examples: The frail old man needed support.
The frail bridge swayed in the wind.
etymology: from Latin fragilis 'breakable', from frangere (to break) + -ilis.

similar.description: both from frangere (break); frail is weak, fragile is easily broken.

memory_tip: frange(破) → 脆弱的、衰弱的。

examples: The parents were frantic with worry.
He made a frantic search for the keys.
etymology: from Old French frentique, from Latin phreneticus 'delirious', from Greek phren (mind).

similar.description: both from ecstasy roots; frantic is panicked, fanatic is zealous.

memory_tip: 失去理智般 → 疯狂的、慌乱的。

etymology: from Latin hereditarius, from hereditas (inheritance), from heres (heir); 'passed by inheritance'.

similar.description: hereditary is the adjective, heredity the noun (inheritance of traits).

memory_tip: heres(继承人) → 遗传的、世袭的。

examples: The church branded him a heretic.
She was called a heretic for her views.
etymology: from Greek hairetikos 'able to choose', from hairein (take/choose); 'one holding dissenting belief'.

similar.description: distinguish from 'heroic'; heretic is a dissenter.

memory_tip: 异端者、持异见者，记“选错信仰”。

examples: The crowd was heterogeneous in age and origin.
A heterogeneous mixture contains different parts.
etymology: from Greek heteros (different) + genos (kind) + -ous; 'of different kinds'.

similar.description: opposite; heterogeneous is mixed, homogeneous is uniform.

memory_tip: hetero(异)+gen(类) → 异质的、混杂的。

examples: The comedy was absolutely hilarious.
We found the mishap hilarious.
etymology: from Greek hilaros 'cheerful, merry' + -ious; 'extremely funny'.

similar.description: unrelated; hilarious is very funny, hysterical is wildly emotional.

memory_tip: hilar(欢乐) → 搞笑的、滑稽的。

examples: They climbed the sunny hillside.
A house perched on the hillside.
etymology: compound of hill + side; 'the slope of a hill'.

similar.description: from hill + side; compare mountainside.

memory_tip: hill(山)+side → 山坡。

examples: We hitchhiked across the country.
He had to hitchhike home after the bus left.
etymology: from hitch (to hook/attach) + hike (to walk); 'to travel by free rides'.

similar.description: hitchhike includes hike; means to get rides while traveling.

memory_tip: hitch(搭)+hike(走) → 搭便车旅行。

examples: The beekeeper opened the hive.
The office was a hive of activity.
etymology: from Old English hufe 'a bee-skep (basket)'; of Germanic origin.

similar.description: distinguish from 'hive' vs 'hive off' (to separate a group).

memory_tip: 蜂箱、忙碌场所，记蜜蜂窝。

examples: Painting is her favourite hobby.
He took up guitar as a hobby.
etymology: from Middle English hoby 'small horse' (hobbyhorse), later a favourite pastime.

similar.description: hobby is singular, hobbies plural.

memory_tip: 由“小马玩具”引申 → 爱好。

examples: Please hold the door open.
The fortress held against the siege.
etymology: from Old English healdan 'to keep, grasp', from Proto-Germanic *haldan.

similar.description: distinguish from 'host' etc.; hold is grasp/keep.

memory_tip: 古英语healdan，握住、保持、容纳。

examples: The war threatened a nuclear holocaust.
The Holocaust is remembered each year.
etymology: from Greek holokauston 'wholly burnt', from holos (whole) + kaustos (burnt); 'total destruction by fire'.

similar.description: distinguish from 'hellish'; holocaust is wholesale burning/destruction.

memory_tip: holo(全)+caust(烧) → 大屠杀、浩劫。

examples: She lived with a family during her homestay.
The homestay gave her real language practice.
etymology: compound of home + stay; 'staying in a local home, esp. as a guest/student'.

similar.description: homestead is a house/farm, homestay is lodging with a family.

memory_tip: home(家)+stay → 寄宿家庭、在家住宿。

examples: The case was treated as a homicide.
Homicide rates fell this year.
etymology: from Latin homo (man) + -cida (killer, from caedere 'to kill'); 'the killing of a human'.

similar.description: both -cide (kill); homicide kills a person, genocide a people.

memory_tip: homi(人)+cide(杀) → 杀人（者）。

examples: They spent their honeymoon in Italy.
The political honeymoon soon ended.
etymology: from honey + moon (month); originally the 'sweet' first month of marriage.

similar.description: honeymoon includes honey (sweet); a post-wedding trip/period.

memory_tip: honey(甜)+moon(月) → 蜜月。

examples: Growth hormone affects height.
Stress releases the hormone cortisol.
etymology: from Greek horman 'to set in motion, urge', from horme (impulse); 'a chemical messenger'.

similar.description: unrelated; hormone is a bodily chemical, harmony is agreement.

memory_tip: horm(冲动/激发) → 荷尔蒙、激素。

examples: Horticulture includes fruit and flower growing.
She studied horticulture at college.
etymology: from Latin hortus (garden) + culture (cultivation); 'garden cultivation'.

similar.description: both -culture; horticulture is garden crops, agriculture is field farming.

memory_tip: hort(园)+culture → 园艺。

examples: The villagers were warm and hospitable.
A hospitable climate welcomes tourists.
etymology: from Latin hospes (guest/host) + -able; 'welcoming to guests'.

similar.description: both from hospes (guest); hospitable is welcoming, hospital is a care house.

memory_tip: hospes(客人) → 好客的、宜人的。

examples: She was taken to the hospital.
The old hospital was converted to flats.
etymology: from Latin hospitale 'guest house', from hospes (guest/stranger); originally a shelter for travellers.

similar.description: both from hospes; hospital is the institution.

memory_tip: hospes(客) → 医院（原为接待所）。

examples: The city is a transport hub.
The hub of the wheel was broken.
etymology: 16th century, of uncertain origin; perhaps from hubbe (a measure of grain); 'central point'.

similar.description: hub is centre, hubbub is noise/confusion.

memory_tip: 中心、枢纽，记轮轴中心。

examples: A hubbub filled the crowded market.
The hubbub of the party grew loud.
etymology: 16th century, imitative of confused noise; 'a loud mixed uproar'.

similar.description: hubbub is noise, hub is a central point.

memory_tip: 嘈杂声、喧闹，拟声。

examples: He quit the humdrum office job.
Life became humdrum without challenge.
etymology: from hum (low sound) + drum (repetitive beat); 'monotonous, dull'.

similar.description: humdrum combines hum + drum; means dull routine.

memory_tip: hum(嗡)+drum(鼓) → 单调的、乏味的。

examples: The camel has a single hump.
He humped the bag onto his back.
etymology: from Middle Dutch homp 'a lump'; 'a rounded protuberance'.

similar.description: similar; hump is a rounded bump, lump is a mass.

memory_tip: 驼峰、隆起，记驼背隆起。

examples: The runner cleared every hurdle.
We overcame the final hurdle.
They hurdle the fence in the race.
etymology: from Old English hyrdel 'a portable fence'; 'a barrier to jump'.

similar.description: unrelated; hurdle is a barrier, hurtle is to move fast.

memory_tip: 栏架、障碍，记跨栏(hurdle)。

examples: He has a deep husky voice.
The husky dog pulled the sled.
She felt husky after the cold.
etymology: from husk (outer covering) + -y; 'dry, rough, or strong like a husk'.

similar.description: husky is the adjective from husk (outer shell).

memory_tip: husk(外壳) → 沙哑的、强壮的（或哈士奇）。

examples: Hydraulic brakes use fluid pressure.
The hydraulic lift raised the car.
etymology: from Greek hydor (water) + aulos (pipe) + -ic; 'operated by water pressure'.

similar.description: hydraulic shares hydro- (water) root.

memory_tip: hydr(水)+aul(管) → 水力的、液压的。

examples: Good hygiene prevents disease.
Kitchen hygiene is essential.
Dental hygiene matters for health.
etymology: from Greek hygieia 'health', from hygies (healthy); 'the science of health'.

similar.description: hygiene is the noun, hygienic the adjective.

memory_tip: hygi(健康) → 卫生。

examples: Hypnosis helped her quit smoking.
The patient entered a state of hypnosis.
etymology: from Greek hypnos 'sleep' + -osis; coined from hypnotize; 'artificial sleep'.

similar.description: distinguish from 'hypothesis'; hypnosis is trance, hypothesis is a theory.

memory_tip: hypn(睡眠) → 催眠（状态）。

examples: His habit of humming is an idiosyncrasy.
Every culture has its idiosyncrasies.
etymology: from Greek idios 'own, personal' + syn- (together) + krasis 'mix, temperament'; 'a personal peculiarity'.

similar.description: unrelated; idiosyncrasy is a quirk, idolatry is worship of idols.

memory_tip: idio(个人)+krasis(混合) → 个人怪癖。

examples: The poem is a pastoral idyll.
Their holiday was a peaceful idyll.
etymology: from Greek eidyllion 'little picture', diminutive of eidos (form); 'a peaceful, simple scene'.

similar.description: unrelated; idyll is a rustic scene, idol is an image worshipped.

memory_tip: 小画卷 → 田园诗、恬静场景。

examples: Turn the key to start the ignition.
The ignition of the fuel caused the blast.
etymology: from Latin ignis 'fire' + -ition; 'the act of setting alight'.

similar.description: ignition is the noun, ignite the verb (from ignis, fire).

memory_tip: ign(火) → 点火、引燃。

examples: His argument was completely illogical.
An illogical fear gripped her.
etymology: from in- (not) + logical; 'not according to logic'.

similar.description: contrast with 'alogical'; illogical means lacking logic.

memory_tip: il(不)+logical → 不合逻辑的。

examples: A storm is imminent.
The threat of war was imminent.
etymology: from Latin imminere 'to overhang, threaten', from in- + minere (project); 'hanging over, about to happen'.

similar.description: often confused; imminent is about to happen, eminent is distinguished/famous.

memory_tip: im(upon)+mine(突出) → 悬在头上 → 迫近的。

examples: Snow impeded our progress.
Regulations should not impede innovation.
etymology: from Latin impedire 'to entangle the feet', from in- + pes/ped- (foot); 'hinder'.

similar.description: impede is the verb, impediment the noun (a hindrance).

memory_tip: im+ped(脚) → 缠住脚 → 阻碍。

examples: His impetuous decision cost him dearly.
She is youthful and impetuous.
etymology: from Latin impetuosus, from impetus 'attack, rush', from petere (to seek); 'rushing, impulsive'.

similar.description: both from impetus; impetuous is rash, impetus is driving force.

memory_tip: impetus(冲动) → 冲动的、鲁莽的。

examples: Doctors implanted a pacemaker.
The idea was implanted in his mind.
etymology: from in- (into) + plant (to fix/plant); 'to insert or embed'.

similar.description: distinguish from 'implied'; implant is to insert, imply is to suggest.

memory_tip: im(入)+plant(种) → 植入、灌输。

examples: The castle was an imposing sight.
She had an imposing manner.
etymology: from in- (upon) + pose + -ing; 'placing upon, commanding attention by size'.

similar.description: imposing is the adjective from impose (to place upon).

memory_tip: im+pose(放) → 使人印象深刻的、宏伟的。

examples: The thief was imprisoned for a year.
Fear imprisoned her spirit.
They sought to imprison the rebel leader.
etymology: from in- (in) + prison; 'to put in prison'.

similar.description: imprison is the verb formed from prison.

memory_tip: im(入)+prison → 监禁、关押。

examples: He gave an impromptu speech.
We held an impromptu picnic.
She sang impromptu at the party.
etymology: from Latin in promptu 'in readiness', from in- + promptus (ready); 'done without preparation'.

similar.description: impromptu from in promptu (ready); means spontaneous.

memory_tip: in promptu(准备好) → 即兴的、即席的。

examples: The actor had to improvise when he forgot his line.
We improvised a meal from leftovers.
etymology: from Latin improvisus 'unforeseen', from in- (not) + provisus (foreseen); 'act without preparation'.

similar.description: unrelated in sense; improvise is extemporize, improve is make better.

memory_tip: im(未)+provis(预见) → 未预见的 → 即兴创作。
